name: Burnt orange
lede: Burnt orange is a deep, reddish orange named in the spirit of burnt sienna and burnt umber, earth pigments darkened by fire.

sections.title: Named after fire
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines burnt orange simply as a reddish orange [1]. The "burnt" in the name follows a pigment habit: burnt ochre is a light brown made by treating ochre with fire, burnt sienna a dark reddish brown, and burnt umber a reddish brown from roasting umber [1]. Those names describe a heated earth. Burnt orange borrows the word for the look of a scorched, reddened hue, not for any material roasted to make it.

In our library the name goes back to the 1930 Maerz and Paul dictionary and to the 1955 ISCC-NBS system, where this swatch sits about 5.5 units from the block called "deep orange" [2]. Our earliest dated record is 1915 [3].

sections.title: The color of the 1970s
sections.body: As environmental worry grew in the early 1970s, with Greenpeace taking that name in 1972, consumer goods were dressed in a back-to-nature palette of burnt orange, harvest gold and, above all, avocado [4]. Clothing, kitchen appliances, baths and even cars were colonized by these shades [4]. They now read as dated [4]. The look is in our own data as [[look:seventies-earth|the seventies earth palette]], and its neighbors include [[harvest-gold]], [[avocado]] and [[rust-orange]] [4].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color near this swatch appears in 64 paintings, and in 63 by the stricter within-painting measure [3]. It almost always plays an accent: 97 per cent of those 63 works [3]. Think of the small orange of a robe, a flame or a fruit rather than a background.

It peaks in the 1400s, in 0.5 per cent of the 945 paintings we hold from that century, about 1.5 times the expected rate [3]. Our earliest match is a work of 1250, which is 665 years before the name's first record, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not proof of a pigment [3]. For a modern comparison see [[painting:commons-Q16689630|the earliest match in the archive]], and [[sienna]] if you want the pigment itself [3].
